pairs.rationale: Acts reports Hellenist widows overlooked in daily service; the letter assigns widow assistance to believing relatives and the Church. This concerns practical community support, without supplying the Acts widows' ages, family circumstances or an identical dispute.

The apostles seek to preserve word service while others handle tables; Jethro advises Moses to share lesser judgments so the burden is bearable. The tasks and leaders differ; the comparison does not make the seven judges or identify their office.

Both select qualified men for delegated responsibilities. Acts specifies seven, reputation, Spirit and wisdom; Exodus specifies able, God-fearing righteous men who hate arrogance and different numerical ranks. These qualifications and duties are preserved rather than made identical.

The apostles devote themselves to prayer and word service. Colossians urges persevering prayer, including prayer that God open a door for the word and its clear proclamation. The apostles' commitment and the community's requested prayers have different speakers and roles.

The selection list includes Philip; the later Caesarea account explicitly calls Philip the evangelist one of the seven. This identifies a concrete later reference to the seven-member appointment, without independently verifying every other listed name or making Philip one of the Twelve.

Both appointments include prayer and laying on hands before assigned work. Acts 13 additionally names fasting and the Spirit's call of Barnabas and Saul; Acts 6 presents the seven before the apostles. The people, tasks and stated initiating actions differ.

Both summary notices say the word of God grew. Acts 6 additionally specifies Jerusalem disciples and many priests obeying the faith; Acts 12 says grew and multiplied after a different episode. The groups, periods and numerical extent are not equated.

Both describe signs and wonders among the people. Acts 6 names Stephen, full of grace and power; Acts 5 attributes such works to the apostles' hands. This repeated ministry description does not turn Stephen into one of the Twelve.

Jesus promises mouth and wisdom that opponents cannot resist or contradict; Stephen's opponents cannot withstand his wisdom and the Spirit with which he speaks. The specific opposition-and-wisdom correspondence is retained while Jesus' promise and the Spirit-associated narration keep their distinct forms.

Stephen's opponents secretly procure a blasphemy allegation; Matthew explicitly describes the council seeking false testimony against Jesus. The accused people and alleged words differ. The comparison concerns manufactured testimony in these confrontations, without endorsing either reported accusation.

Both describe Jesus' witnesses brought before the council. Stephen is seized amid stirred-up opposition; the earlier apostles are brought without force because officers fear the people. These contrasting seizure details and different hearings are kept distinct.

Both accounts explicitly label witnesses false and include charges concerning the sacred place. Mark reports a sanctuary-demolition/rebuilding allegation against Jesus; Acts alleges Stephen speaks against this holy place and the law. Neither accusation becomes the narrator's endorsement.

The witnesses allege Stephen said Jesus would destroy this place and change Mosaic customs. John reports Jesus telling His hearers to destroy the sanctuary and promising to raise it, with the narrator explaining His body. Speakers, agency, object and stated claims are not interchanged.

The council sees Stephen's face like an angel's face; Manoah's wife describes a visitor's appearance like God's messenger, very glorious. These are specific messenger-like appearance descriptions, not a claim that Stephen is an angel or that Acts explicitly describes rays or a veil.

Both council narratives have the high priest question the accused after testimony. Matthew asks Jesus about the witnesses and then His identity, with silence reported; Acts asks Stephen whether the charges are true before his speech. No identical wording, priest identity or hearing is asserted.

Stephen locates God's appearance before Haran, in Mesopotamia. Genesis narrates an appearance near Shechem after Abram has entered Canaan. Both concern divine appearance to Abraham, but their stated settings and stages are not collapsed into the same appearance.

Stephen's leave-land-and-relatives and shown-land command corresponds to the Lord's command to Abram. Genesis additionally names departure from the father's house. Its narrative placement and Stephen's preceding Mesopotamia notice are not silently rewritten.

Genesis narrates Terah taking the family from the Chaldeans to Haran and records his death there; its following account describes Abram's departure to Canaan. Stephen explicitly says God moved Abraham after his father's death. The distinct agencies and chronological notices remain, without additional birth-order or age arithmetic.

Genesis combines Abram's childlessness, a promised heir and seed, and God's giving this land to inherit. Stephen joins childlessness with promised possession and says no footstep's inheritance was given then. The target does not independently state that last measurement.

Both predict Abraham's seed living as strangers and suffering enslavement and affliction for four hundred years. Stephen's compressed formulation and the saved Genesis wording are preserved, without substituting a different chronological total.

The judgment of the enslaving nation and the descendants' departure correspond to Genesis. Genesis adds much baggage; Stephen adds worship in this place. That worship clause is not attributed to this Genesis unit.

God's promise to Moses joins bringing the people from Egypt with serving God on this mountain; Stephen joins departure with worship in this place. This supplies a specific related promise while retaining mountain versus place and their different recipients and contexts.

Both name Abraham fathering Isaac and circumcising him on the eighth day. Genesis names Sarah and obedience to God's command; Stephen situates this in the covenant and continues through Jacob and the patriarchs. The later genealogy is not independently supplied by these two target units.

Both place Joseph in Egypt after sale and affirm God's presence with him. Genesis names the Ishmaelites and Potiphar; Stephen stresses the patriarchs' jealousy and sale. Their different actor descriptions and emphases are kept rather than reduced to an identical sentence.

Pharaoh recognizes Joseph's God-given discernment and places him over his house and Egypt. Stephen summarizes divine rescue, favor, wisdom and that promotion. Genesis supplies the specific appointment, not a separate complete account of every affliction mentioned in Stephen's summary.

Both explicitly describe famine affecting Egypt and Canaan with severe distress. Stephen adds the fathers' lack of provisions; Genesis describes the lands languishing after Jacob's arrival. This does not identify the exact stage of the famine or equate the family's provisions at each stage.

Both describe Jacob hearing of Egyptian grain and sending sons to obtain it. Genesis specifies ten brothers, whereas Stephen says our fathers and marks the first journey. The earlier twelve-patriarch list is not substituted for Genesis's ten travelers.

Genesis narrates Joseph making himself known to his brothers and their troubled response; Stephen places recognition on the second visit and also mentions the family becoming known to Pharaoh. The target's hearing of weeping in Pharaoh's house is not treated as a verbatim account of that latter family notice.

Stephen's summons mentions seventy-five persons; the supplied Greek-based Genesis totals Jacob's house entering Egypt at seventy-five, alongside sixty-six and nine in its breakdown. The stated scenes and groupings remain distinct; neither total is replaced with seventy or forced into an unstated individual roster.

Stephen summarizes Jacob's descent and the deaths of Jacob and the fathers; Genesis narrates Jacob dying after his burial instructions. This specifically supports the Jacob-death component, not every ancestor's death or the entire migration chronology.

pairs.relationship: Shechem purchase comparison with unresolved differences
pairs.rationale: Both mention a Shechem/Hamor purchase, but Stephen says Abraham bought a tomb from Hamor's sons for silver; Genesis names Jacob buying a field from Hamor, father of Shechem, for a hundred lambs. Buyer, object, seller description and price differ; no reconciliation or replacement is supplied.

Both describe Israel's growth and multiplication in Egypt. Stephen relates this to the approaching promise's time; Exodus emphasizes the people's great numerical strength. The target does not independently supply Stephen's particular promise-timing explanation.
Both introduce another Egyptian king who did not know Joseph. This is a direct narrative correspondence; no extra royal name, dynasty or date is inferred.

Stephen describes oppression forcing exposure of infants so they would not live. Exodus explicitly commands throwing Hebrew male children into the river while keeping females alive. The sex-specific command and method are retained rather than silently expanded into Stephen's more compressed formulation.

Both describe Moses' beauty and three months of concealment or upbringing. Stephen says beautiful before God and in his father's house; Exodus describes the child's beauty and states 'they hid him.' The evaluators, wording, and parental actions remain distinct.

Both describe Pharaoh's daughter receiving Moses and his becoming her son. Exodus gives the basket discovery, compassion, paid nursing by his mother and later presentation when he grew; Stephen compresses these stages into rescue and upbringing. The additional stages are not erased.

Stephen describes Moses as powerful in words and deeds; the travelers describe Jesus as a prophet mighty in deed and word before God and the people. This is a bounded description comparison between different figures, not evidence that Jesus received Moses' Egyptian education.

Both describe Moses going out to his Israelite brothers when grown. Stephen specifies forty years and his inward resolve; Exodus describes seeing their suffering and an Egyptian striking a Hebrew. Neither the age nor the inward explanation is inserted into Exodus.

Both narrate Moses seeing an Egyptian wronging a Hebrew and striking the Egyptian down. Exodus adds looking around and hiding him in sand; Stephen calls the act defense and vengeance for the oppressed man. Those evaluative and action details are not made identical.

Stephen first reports Moses' supposition that his brothers understood deliverance through him, then later affirms God's sending of the very rejected Moses as ruler and redeemer. Presumption at the earlier encounter and later divine commission are distinct; the link does not supply divine approval of the Egyptian's killing.

Both place Moses before fighting Hebrews on the next day. Exodus addresses the wrongdoer about striking his neighbor; Stephen presents a brotherhood appeal and attempted reconciliation. The formulations are related without assigning equal guilt to both men.

The who-made-you-ruler-and-judge challenge corresponds to Exodus. Stephen additionally narrates the wrongdoer pushing Moses away; that physical action is not inserted into the target's spoken objection.
Both report the objection asking whether Moses would kill the speaker as he killed the Egyptian yesterday. This is the reported question, not a prediction that Moses intended another killing.

Both describe flight to Midian, settlement and fatherhood. Exodus adds Pharaoh's death threat, the well encounter, marriage and Gershom's birth; Stephen attributes flight to the saying and mentions two sons. This target names one son's birth rather than independently narrating both.

The later Exodus notice explicitly names Moses' wife and two sons, Gershom and Eliezer, whose names recall sojourning and deliverance from Pharaoh. This supplies the two-son counterpart without independently dating both births to Stephen's Midian interval.

Both describe an angel appearing in a fiery bush to Moses in the wilderness setting. Exodus names Horeb and his shepherding; Stephen names Sinai and a forty-year interval. The names, chronology and angel description are preserved without adding an elapsed period to Exodus.

Both describe Moses approaching to examine the remarkable bush and the Lord's voice addressing him. Exodus quotes the repeated Moses call; Stephen describes marveling and then introduces the following divine words. The formulations are not treated as a single identical quotation.

Both identify the speaker as the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob and describe Moses' fear of looking. Stephen says he trembled and did not dare look closely; Exodus says he turned his face away. These responses are kept as written.
Both command removal of footwear because the standing place is holy ground. Exodus additionally says not to approach nearer; Stephen's shorter citation does not reproduce that prohibition.

Both join God's seeing Egypt's affliction, hearing suffering, coming down to rescue and sending Moses. Exodus says cry and explicitly sends him to Pharaoh; Stephen says groaning and Egypt. Its compressed citation does not replace those distinct expressions.

Stephen explicitly repeats the earlier who-appointed-you-ruler-and-judge rejection while asserting God's subsequent sending of that same Moses. The earlier human objection and the later divine commissioning are opposed within one speech, not independent records.

Stephen's summary includes the sea deliverance; Exodus describes Israel crossing on dry ground, rescue from the Egyptians and trust in God and Moses. This concretely illustrates the sea component, without making the target itself narrate all Egyptian signs or the forty wilderness years.
Stephen's promised prophet like Moses from the brothers corresponds to Moses' promise in Deuteronomy. The target also commands hearing him; it does not itself name Jesus in this unit.

Both concern the wilderness reception and transmission of God's instruction through Moses. Deuteronomy describes the Lord's fire-voice, covenant and teaching commands; Stephen names an angel, Sinai's assembly and living oracles. The angel and Lord formulations are not silently made identical.

Stephen describes refusal of Moses and hearts turning toward Egypt in his calf account; Numbers records a later complaint and proposal to appoint a leader and return to Egypt. This compares rejection and Egyptian nostalgia, without identifying the occasions or spoken proposals.

Both ask Aaron for gods to go before them and profess ignorance of what happened to Moses who led them out of Egypt. Exodus explicitly introduces Moses' delay; the quoted objection remains the people's speech.

Both describe the made calf, sacrifice and celebration. Exodus narrates Aaron's making, altar, offerings, eating and play; Stephen stresses an idol and rejoicing in their handwork. The descriptions are compared without endorsing the calf's divine claim.

Stephen's forty-year wilderness sacrifice question corresponds to Amos' question addressed to Israel. Stephen's preceding interpretation about God handing people over to heaven's host is not presented as wording contained in this single Amos unit.

Both mention Moloch's tent, Raiphan's star, made images and deportation. The supplied Amos says beyond Damascus; Acts says beyond Babylon. Those different destination names remain explicit rather than being silently harmonized.

Both connect the sanctuary or tabernacle's making with a revealed pattern shown to Moses on the mountain. Exodus also names vessel patterns and God's appearing among the people; Stephen emphasizes the wilderness Tent of Testimony. Their additional details remain distinct.

Stephen describes the inherited Tent entering the occupied land with Joshua; Joshua describes the congregation pitching the Tabernacle of Testimony at Shiloh while the land was under their control. The target does not independently supply the entry sequence or Stephen's until-David limit.

The psalm recalls David's vow to find the Lord a place and a dwelling for the God of Jacob. Stephen speaks of David's favor and seeking a dwelling for the house of Jacob. The house-of-Jacob and God-of-Jacob expressions, and request versus vow, remain distinct.

Both explicitly attribute building the Lord's house to Solomon. Kings supplies its dimensions; Stephen gives a short ancestral summary. No familiar alternative measurements are substituted for the saved target.

Stephen says the Most High does not dwell in things made by hands; Paul's later speech says the world-making God does not dwell in sanctuaries made by hands. The parallel is a specific divine-dwelling claim in different addresses, not identification of their audiences or every worship practice.
Both declare heaven God's throne and earth His footstool, then question what house or resting place people can build. The speaker and creation-and-house imagery correspond directly.

Stephen's question about God's hand making all these things corresponds to Isaiah's declaration that His hand made them. Isaiah continues with their belonging to Him and regard for humble hearers; those additions are not inserted into Stephen's shorter question.

Stephen calls his hearers stiff-necked and uncircumcised in hearts and ears; Deuteronomy commands circumcising heart-hardness and ceasing to stiffen the neck. This is a specific paired moral image, not a claim about physical circumcision or every Jewish person.

Stephen charges his hearers with resisting the Holy Spirit as their fathers did; Isaiah recalls ancestors disobeying and provoking God's holy spirit. The ancestral-disobedience correspondence does not make every episode or consequence identical.

Jesus' address connects the fathers' killing prophets with later persecution of God's messengers; Stephen charges his hearers with ancestral persecution and betrayal and murder of the Righteous One. The addressed groups, stages and titles remain distinct, without extending the accusation to an ethnicity.

Both explicitly associate the law with angelic mediation. Stephen charges his hearers with not keeping it; Galatians discusses transgressions, the promised seed and a mediator. The different arguments and singular/plural angel descriptions in Stephen's wider speech are not collapsed.

Both council hearings produce an enraged reaction to testimony and deadly hostility. Acts 7 adds teeth-grinding toward Stephen; Acts 5 reports the desire to kill the apostles. These are separate hearings and different reported expressions of rage.

Stephen sees God's glory and Jesus standing at God's right hand while full of the Holy Spirit; Jesus' earlier saying places the Son of Man seated at the right hand of God's power. The identity-and-position correspondence preserves standing versus seated and vision versus promise.

Both explicitly place the Son of Man at God's right hand. Stephen reports opened heavens and standing; Jesus predicts being seated from now on. The posture, wording and speakers are not treated as identical.

Stephen's hearers physically stop their ears after his charge of uncircumcised ears and resisting the Spirit. This links a specific earlier moral image with the narrated reaction, while keeping metaphor, physical action and the crowd's unreported private motives distinct.

Paul later recalls Stephen's bloodshed, his own approval and guarding the killers' garments, corresponding to the Saul-and-garments notice. The later statement does not separately repeat every city-exit or stoning detail, and is a retrospect within Acts.

Both dying speakers entrust their spirit in prayer. Stephen addresses Lord Jesus and asks Him to receive it; Jesus addresses the Father and entrusts His spirit into His hands. The addressees and exact petitions are kept distinct.

Stephen asks the Lord not to hold this sin against them; Jesus asks the Father to forgive them because they do not know what they do. The mercy petitions are related, but Stephen's kneeling and falling asleep are not inserted into Jesus' crucifixion prayer.

Paul later recalls standing by and approving Stephen's bloodshed while guarding the killers' garments. This corresponds specifically to Saul's approval here; the later recollection does not independently repeat the whole Church-dispersion notice or the apostles' exception.

Devout men bury Stephen with great lamentation; Jacob's burial narrative likewise combines burial with great mourning. The mourners and narrative settings differ; Genesis gives seven days of mourning, while Acts states no duration here. This is a funerary-action comparison, not an identification of either burial company or rite.

The letter recalls ravaging the Church of God and persecution beyond measure, corresponding to Saul's church-ravaging activity. Acts additionally narrates entering houses and imprisoning men and women. The retrospective does not independently describe every house raid.

The later notice explicitly traces dispersed word-proclaimers to the affliction over Stephen, extending travel to Phoenicia, Cyprus and Antioch. It recalls the same dispersion-and-proclamation development without making its later destinations identical to the earlier regional summary.

Samaria is explicitly included in Jesus' announced witness geography; Philip's proclamation of the Christ in Samaria fits that geographical extension. This does not place Philip among the particular original hearers of the promise or make every detail of his mission explicit there.

Philip's speech and visible signs attract concerted attention; the later mission likewise links the Lord's gracious word with granted signs, but its city is divided. The common word/sign association does not imply identical audiences or a universally uniform response.

Both narrate unclean spirits coming out with loud cries. Mark concerns one man at Jesus' command; Acts concerns many during Philip's ministry and also other healings. The agents, numbers, bodily conditions and additional actions are not merged.

Both describe joy in connection with the gospel's reception. Samaria's city rejoices after the narrated signs and healings; the later Gentile hearers rejoice and glorify the word. Acts 8 does not thereby declare that every city resident shares every belief statement of the later group.

Both narratives introduce a named magician in a setting reached by Christian proclamation. Simon's self-importance and Samarian influence differ from Bar-Jesus/Elymas' proconsular association and active opposition to faith. These are different figures, not independent attestations of Simon's particular claims.

Both report audiences assigning extraordinary God-associated status to people. Simon receives the Power-of-God title; the Lycaonians identify Barnabas and Paul with gods and prepare sacrifice. These are reported claims with different wording and actions, not identical theological beliefs endorsed by the narrator.

Simon formerly astonished the people through magic; later Simon himself is astonished while seeing signs and great works after staying close to Philip. This is an internal reversal of who is astonished. The long duration belongs only to the earlier magic, and the later belief-and-baptism sequence precedes the stated astonishment; the sources of astonishment and any final assessment of his faith are not equated.

Both describe hearing the Christian message, believing and baptism. Acts 8 names Philip's kingdom-and-Jesus proclamation and men and women; Acts 18 names Crispus, his household and many Corinthians. The stated groups, ministers and demographic details are not transferred.

John explicitly describes people believing while seeing signs and then says Jesus did not entrust Himself to them. Acts states Simon's belief and baptism, then describes his astonishment at signs and great works. The sequence and stated reactions differ; neither account supplies an additional verdict here about the other group's faith.

Both accounts describe Jerusalem hearing of reception in another mission region and sending representatives. The apostles send Peter and John toward Samaria; the Church sends Barnabas as far as Antioch. The sending bodies, destinations and delegates remain distinct.

Peter and John pray that others receive the Holy Spirit; Jesus teaches that the Father gives the Holy Spirit to those who ask Him. The promise and this intercession are related without making their speakers, recipients or narrated timing identical.

Samaria is already baptized into the Lord Jesus' name before the Spirit has fallen upon them. Cornelius' hearers receive the Spirit before Peter orders baptism in Jesus Christ's name. These explicitly different sequences are preserved rather than turned into one universal order.

Both associate laying on hands with the Holy Spirit's reception or coming. Acts 8 names the visiting apostles; Acts 19 names Paul after baptism into the Lord Jesus' name and adds tongues and prophecy. Those extra manifestations are not inserted into Acts 8.

Simon's money offer receives Peter's rebuke for thinking God's gift could be acquired with money. This identifies the stated meaning and rejection of the offer in the same exchange, not an independently attested transaction or a successful purchase.

Simon asks for authority to impart the Spirit through his hands, the action he has just observed when the apostles lay hands and people receive the Spirit. The preceding event supplies his request's concrete referent; it does not grant him that authority.

Peter rebukes treating God's gift as purchasable; Jesus directs freely received healing and liberating ministry to be freely given. The gift types and immediate instructions differ, and the comparison does not supply a completed sale or every rule about material ministry support.

Peter says Simon's heart is not upright before God; the psalm describes a heart not upright with Him and covenant unfaithfulness. The shared moral description does not identify Simon with every person or event in the psalm's ancestral account.

Both call for turning from wicked ways or counsels toward God and forgiveness. Peter specifically urges repentance and prayer concerning the heart's intention, with perhaps; Isaiah calls people to God and promises mercy upon return. The different formulations do not narrate Simon's subsequent forgiveness.

Peter describes bitter gall and a bond of unrighteousness; Deuteronomy warns about a root springing in gall and bitterness amid turning to foreign gods. The paired bitter/gall image corresponds, while root, bond and each person's situation remain distinct.

The returning witnesses are the Peter-and-John delegation previously sent from Jerusalem to Samaria. Their return and village proclamation develop that commission's narrative course, without making the earlier sending notice an independent record of all their later teaching stops.

Both angelic communications direct movements that lead to gospel instruction. Philip is sent to the desert Gaza road; Cornelius is directed to summon Peter from Joppa. The commanded travelers, locations and angelic wording remain distinct.

Isaiah addresses eunuchs and foreigners with promises concerning God's house and prayer, including covenant conditions. Acts introduces an Ethiopian eunuch returning from Jerusalem worship. This supplies relevant inclusion-and-worship background without independently verifying his observance of every named condition or assigning an unstated legal status.

The narrator later quotes the Isaiah passage this traveler is reading. That identifies the text behind the earlier Isaiah-reading notice, without independently verifying the chariot journey or reconstructing every other passage he may have read.

The Spirit directs Philip to approach the chariot and Peter to accompany the waiting men. These are concrete mission-encounter directions with different recipients and actions; the earlier angelic communications are not collapsed into the Spirit's spoken instructions.

Philip asks whether the hearer understands the Isaiah reading; Nehemiah narrates reading God's law, Esdras teaching and explaining, and the people understanding. The individual question and the public law-reading scene differ, while reading with understanding is a specific common concern.

The traveler asks for guidance and invites Philip beside him; Nehemiah describes Esdras' explanation accompanying the law reading so the people understand. The books, audiences and forms of instruction differ; the comparison does not reconstruct Philip's whole explanation.

Both describe the silent sheep led to slaughter and lamb before its shearer. Isaiah also begins with affliction. This is the quoted textual correspondence, distinct from any later explanation of the passage's referent.

The humiliation, removed judgment, generation question and life taken from earth correspond to Isaiah's supplied wording. Isaiah additionally states being led to death because of the people's iniquities; that continuation is not inserted into Acts' shorter citation.

The eunuch asks whom the prophet means; the next narration says Philip begins from this Scripture and announces Jesus. This connects the question with the narrated exposition, without inventing a verbatim yes/no answer or making the entire sermon available.

Philip begins with this Isaiah text to announce Jesus; Jesus interprets the things concerning Himself from Moses and all the prophets. The common Scripture-to-Jesus exposition does not identify the complete passage lists or equate the teachers and occasions.

Both ask what could prevent water baptism. The eunuch asks about himself after Philip's proclamation; Peter asks about Cornelius' company after their Spirit reception. The speakers, recipients and stated preceding events differ; the absent Acts 8:37 is not supplied.

Both narrate baptism by another person and movement into or out of water. Acts names Philip and the eunuch going down, followed by baptism; Mark names John baptizing Jesus and Jesus coming up. The participants, sequence descriptions and physical details are not made identical.

Acts narrates the Lord's Spirit snatching Philip away; Obadiah fears the Lord's Spirit will carry Elijah to an unknown land. A narrated removal and an anticipated possibility are distinct, and the target does not independently attest Philip's departure or the eunuch's joy.

Philip's proclamation route ends at Caesarea; the later travel account finds Philip the evangelist, one of the seven, with a house there. This provides a person-and-location continuation without independently attesting Azotus, every intervening town or a stated duration.

Saul's continuing murderous threats against disciples correspond to the letter's recollection of extreme persecution and ravaging the Church. Acts supplies the high-priest approach and immediate threats; the letter does not separately narrate each threatened act.

Paul later recalls persecuting the Way, binding men and women and receiving letters before the Damascus journey to bring people to Jerusalem. The retrospective states received letters and punishment; Acts 9 narrates the request and names the synagogues. These are related reports with distinct wording.

Both describe approaching Damascus and a sudden heavenly light flashing around Saul or the first-person speaker. The later report adds about noon and brilliance; those details are not silently inserted into the earlier narration.

Both report falling and the repeated Saul-name persecution question. Acts 9 here specifies Saul falling; Acts 26 says all fell and adds Hebrew speech and the goads clause. The reports' scope and wording remain, without inventing an unreported sequence or adding goads to Acts 9.

The identity question and Jesus' reply identifying Himself as the persecuted One recur in Paul's later account. Acts 22 adds the Nazarene designation; it is not inserted into Acts 9's shorter self-identification.

Both direct Saul to rise and enter the city to be told his task. Acts 22 names Damascus, adds his what-should-I-do question and says everything appointed; Acts 9 does not repeat those additional words.

pairs.relationship: internal retelling with preserved hearing difference
pairs.rationale: Acts 9 says the companions stood speechless, hearing the voice but seeing no one; Acts 22 says they saw the light but did not hear the voice of the One speaking to Paul. The actual hearing descriptions are preserved, without replacing not-hearing with an unstated failure to understand.

Both describe Saul unable to see and being led by the hand into Damascus. Acts 9 says his eyes were open; Acts 22 attributes inability to the light's brightness. Neither clause is transferred into the other report as its own wording.

The later sight restoration and taking food correspond to the earlier blindness and abstention from food. This tracks the narrative change of condition; the later units neither explicitly report drinking nor independently specify the earlier three-day duration.

Both identify Ananias as the Damascus participant who comes to Saul. Acts 9 calls him a disciple and reports the Lord's vision-address; Acts 22 describes his law-devotion and good reputation. The later report does not independently narrate his initial vision or identify him with another Ananias.

Saul is identified as from Tarsus; the later Paul self-description names Tarsus in Cilicia. Acts 13:9 explicitly supplies the Saul/Paul name connection. This correspondence does not independently attest Straight Street, Judas's house or the prayer, and no other Judas is identified.

The vision anticipates Ananias entering, laying hands and restored sight; the later narration records the visit, hands and sight recovery. It adds the Jesus message, Spirit-filling purpose and baptism. The vision and outcome belong to the same account, not independent witnesses.

Ananias reports hearing of Saul's harm to the Jerusalem saints; the earlier Jerusalem persecution narrative describes his church raids and imprisonment of men and women. A character's reported information and the narrator's account are kept distinct.

Ananias mentions chief-priest authority to bind those calling Jesus' name; the earlier narrative describes requesting the high priest's letters for Damascus synagogues and people of the Way. The grantor descriptions and group-designations are related without being made verbatim identical.

Jesus tells Ananias that Saul is a chosen vessel bearing His name before Gentiles, kings and Israel; Paul's later account reports Jesus appointing him a servant and witness sent to the people and Gentiles. Recipients, setting and specified audiences differ rather than becoming one speech.

The Lord tells Ananias of Saul's necessary suffering for His name; Paul later describes Spirit testimony that bonds and afflictions await him while completing Jesus' ministry. The voices, times and particular forecasts are distinct, not a claim that every suffering event is listed here.

Both have Ananias come and address Brother Saul before restored sight. Acts 9 adds laying hands, Jesus' sending and the purpose of sight and Spirit filling; Acts 22 quotes regain-your-sight and immediate seeing. Neither report is expanded with the other's unquoted dialogue.

Both narrate or direct sight restoration and baptism in the Ananias encounter. Acts 9 says something like scales fell; Acts 22 supplies calling, witness and washing-sins/name language. The simile and additional words remain in their respective accounts.

Saul takes food and regains strength after deprivation; Elijah eats and drinks and travels in that food's strength after the angel's instruction. The needs, agents and subsequent activities differ, without transferring Elijah's forty-day journey to Saul.

Saul's synagogue proclamation calls Jesus God's Son; the later sermon announces God's promise fulfilled in Jesus and cites the psalm's My-Son declaration. The shorter proclamation and later scriptural argument are distinct occasions and forms.

Both report hearers recognizing the paradox of the former persecutor now proclaiming the faith. Acts quotes Damascus astonishment and the intended prisoner mission; Galatians reports Judean churches hearing and glorifying God. Their communities and reactions are not identified.

Both describe Saul/Paul arguing that the proclaimed Jesus is the Christ among Jewish hearers. Acts 17 specifies Thessalonica, Scripture reasoning and suffering/resurrection arguments; Acts 9 names Damascus and growing strength. Those detailed arguments are not supplied as the earlier speech's transcript.

Acts describes a Jewish conspiracy to kill Saul in the Damascus context; Paul recalls an ethnarch under Aretas guarding the city to seize him and his escape. The common danger-and-escape setting does not identify the actors, equate capture with killing or supply an unrecorded joint conspiracy.

Acts says Saul learns of a plot and the gates are watched day and night to kill him; the letter names the ethnarch's guarding the city to seize him. The different actors, stated purposes, gate detail and hours remain, without adding them to the letter.

Both describe being lowered through the wall in a basket or hamper to escape. Acts names disciples and night; the letter specifies a window and escape from the official's hands. Helpers, timing and window detail are retained in their own reports.

Barnabas reports Saul seeing the Lord and the Lord speaking to him; the earlier narrative describes heavenly light and Jesus' identifying voice. This is a retrospective to the encounter, not permission to supply an unreported visible bodily form or change what the companions saw.

Barnabas' report of bold Damascus proclamation refers to the narrated synagogue proclamation and argument that Jesus is the Christ. Boldness is his reported characterization; the earlier units describe proclamation, astonishment and increasing strength rather than quoting that adjective.

Acts describes Saul being with the apostles and moving and speaking in Jerusalem; Galatians names a visit to Cephas and seeing James, with three years and fifteen days. The named contacts and time notices are not inserted into Acts or used to reconstruct every movement.

Saul's Hellenist dispute and their attempted killing are compared with Paul's later Jerusalem vision report warning that people will not accept his testimony and directing departure. The group, murder attempt, temple vision and divine direction remain distinct narrated details rather than one reconstructed dialogue.

The brothers send Saul to Tarsus after bringing him to Caesarea; later Barnabas goes to Tarsus to seek him. This supplies a concrete subsequent person-and-location connection, not independent testimony to the escort route or a specified elapsed interval.

Both summary notices describe the Church or Churches being built up or strengthened and increasing. Acts 9 names peace, fear of the Lord, Spirit encouragement and three regions; Acts 16 specifies strengthened faith and daily numerical increase. Their settings and stated means are not made identical.

The later summons explicitly says Peter was in Lydda and explains its nearness to Joppa, connecting back to this visit among the Lydda saints. It clarifies the narrated location rather than independently attesting all his travels.

Both introduce a paralyzed man associated with a bed or mat. Aeneas has been confined eight years; Luke's men carry another paralyzed man to Jesus. The patients, duration and transport details are distinct, with no congenital condition or eight-year history added to Luke.

Peter attributes Aeneas' healing to Jesus Christ and commands rising and bed-making; earlier he invokes Jesus Christ's name, commands rising and walking and takes the other man's hand. Jesus' agency, different commands, patients and reported manual action are preserved.

Both Peter episodes end with local responses to a restoration. Aeneas is seen by all Lydda and Sharon residents who turn to the Lord; Dorcas' restoration becomes known in Joppa and many believe in the Lord. All versus many and seeing versus report remain distinct.

Dorcas is introduced as a woman disciple full of good works and charity; the letter commends good works as fitting women professing reverence for God, in contrast to costly adornment. This compares stated moral conduct without supplying Dorcas' marriage, age or dress.

Both narratives place a body in an upper room following fatal illness. Acts names Dorcas and washing her; Kings describes the widow's son and Elijah carrying him to his bed. The people and bearer differ; washing is stated only in Acts.

Joppa's disciples send two men for Peter in Lydda; Cornelius later sends two slaves and a soldier for Peter in Joppa after angelic instruction. Both are explicit summons delegations, but callers, numbers, locations and purposes differ.

The weeping widows show clothing Dorcas made while with them, giving concrete context for her earlier good-works and charity description. This is one narrative's characterization and illustration, not proof of every garment's ownership or an independent account of her work.

Both narratives put others outside and command a girl or woman to rise. Peter kneels and prays before addressing Tabitha; Jesus takes the girl's hand and uses the translated Aramaic command, and she walks. Acts names Tabitha, while Mark leaves the girl unnamed; the sequence and bodily responses differ, and Mark's retained passage does not report a prayer.

Peter calls the saints and widows and presents Tabitha alive; Elijah brings the boy down and gives him to his mother, declaring that he lives. The living-person presentation corresponds, without transferring Peter's hand assistance or identifying the recipients and restored people.

Joppa's widespread report is followed by the note that many believed in the Lord; the earlier Aeneas episode describes Lydda and Sharon residents seeing him and turning to the Lord. The report/seeing distinction and many/all formulations are retained rather than counted as identical populations.

The later angelic address identifies Peter lodging with Simon the tanner, whose house is by the sea, corresponding to this Joppa stay. Host Simon remains distinct from the guest Simon Peter; the later instructions do not independently measure many days.

The messengers later name Cornelius as a centurion and describe his character, matching the introduced man. Their report does not independently name the Italian cohort or repeat every location detail; this is an internal person reference.

The narrator describes Cornelius' prayers and alms; the angel then says those prayers and alms have ascended as a memorial before God. The stated practices and response are connected within one story, not independent testimony to every household member's conduct.

Cornelius later recalls praying at the ninth hour and a man in shining clothing standing before him. The initial account calls the visitor an angel seen in a vision; the report adds four-days-ago and clothing. These descriptions and the named hour are retained distinctly.

Both messages join Cornelius' prayer and alms with divine regard. The angel says they ascended as a memorial; Cornelius reports prayer heard and alms remembered. The corresponding message is not reduced to identical wording or a separate independent revelation.

Cornelius' later report repeats sending to Joppa and summoning Simon called Peter. The report also repeats lodging details from the next initial unit. This is the same commission retold, not a second independently attested summons.

The initial angelic address and Cornelius' report both identify the host Simon the tanner and a house beside the sea. The host is kept distinct from the guest Simon Peter; no absent additional promise about what Peter will say is inserted into this address.

Cornelius dispatches two household slaves and a devout soldier; the Spirit later tells Peter three men are seeking him. The count connects the delegation across the narrative, without giving the slaves the soldier's explicitly stated description or supplying their names.

The men sent to Joppa by Cornelius later appear at Simon's gate after asking directions. This connects the narrated dispatch with its arrival, without reconstructing the explanation Cornelius gave or the unquoted travel conversations.

Peter later recalls praying in Joppa and seeing the sheet vision in a trance. Acts 10 additionally specifies the rooftop, sixth hour and travelers approaching. Those details are not imported into the shorter retrospective or confused with Cornelius' ninth-hour prayer.

Both accounts associate Peter's vision with a trance. Acts 10 adds hunger and meal preparation; Peter's later narration foregrounds prayer in Joppa. The different reported circumstances remain rather than supplying a physical explanation for the vision.

Both describe something like a large sheet descending from heaven by four corners. Peter's report says it came right to him; the narrator says lowered to earth and notes opened heaven. The likeness and additional destination details are preserved.

Both vision accounts list four-footed animals, creeping things and birds. Peter's later report explicitly adds wild animals and his examining the contents. These list and action details are retained without pretending both sentences have identical inventories.

Peter's report repeats the voice's Rise-Peter-slaughter-and-eat command. This is an explicit quotation counterpart within Acts, not evidence of another independent voice-event or an additional unreported speaker identification.

Both refusals begin By no means, Lord, but Acts10 says never eaten anything common and unclean; Acts11 says nothing common or unclean has ever entered my mouth. The and/or wording and eaten/entered-my-mouth descriptions remain distinct.

Both second-voice statements forbid calling common what God has cleansed. The report explicitly calls the voice from heaven; the initial narration locates this within the animal vision. The shared wording is not independently applied here to every later question.

Both say the episode happened three times and its object or everything was taken back into heaven. The report's everything and drawn-up-again wording remains distinct from the initial immediately and object notice; no exact repeated subaction is invented.

Both connect the vision's aftermath with Cornelius' delegation arriving at the lodging. Acts 10 gives Peter's perplexity, directions and gate; Acts 11 gives three men and Caesarea as origin. Neither is expanded into a duplicate transcript of the other.

The men ask whether Simon called Peter is lodging there, carrying out the specific search directed by the angel's earlier name and address. The question is not itself proof that every address detail was repeated aloud at the gate.

The later report names three waiting men and the Spirit's direction to accompany them, corresponding to Peter's current Spirit-address during reflection. The count, divine direction and distinct surrounding details remain; this is one encounter retold.

Both give the Spirit's direction to go with the men. Acts 10 says without hesitation and I have sent them; Acts 11 says making no distinction and adds six accompanying brothers. The expressions and stated agency are not silently made verbatim identical.

Peter first asks the arriving men why they came and later asks the assembled hearers why they summoned him. This is a concrete repeated invitation to explain the commission at two stages, with different interlocutors rather than a second unrelated inquiry.

The messengers report an angel directing Cornelius to summon Peter and hear him; the earlier narration supplies the angelic appearance and summons. Their public-reputation description is additional and is not treated as an independently verified census of every Jewish person's judgment.

Peter later says six brothers accompanied him and entered the man's house. Acts 10 says some Joppa brothers went with him after lodging the messengers. The later number and house entry clarify the journey, without being inserted into the initial some notice.

Cornelius gathers relatives and close friends while awaiting Peter; Peter subsequently enters and finds many assembled. This links preparation with the resulting audience, without independently identifying every attendee or assigning them names.

Cornelius falls at Peter's feet and bows; the Lycaonian crowd gives Barnabas and Paul divine names and prepares sacrifice before their human-status response. The actions and professed beliefs differ: Acts 10 does not explicitly say Cornelius identified Peter as a god.

Peter raises Cornelius and says he too is a human being; Barnabas and Paul likewise insist they are humans of the same nature as their hearers. The shared human-status response does not transfer the sacrifice scene or Peter's physical raising action to the other encounter.

The many people Peter finds gathered correspond to Cornelius' preceding assembly of relatives and close friends. This provides a concrete narrative antecedent for the audience, not a new independent attendance count or proof of each person's identity.

Peter expressly applies the common/unclean vocabulary to human beings after God's cleansing command in the vision. The vision's animal setting and Peter's declared human-association application remain distinct, rather than being replaced by an unstated comprehensive legal ruling.

Peter's coming without objection follows the Spirit's instruction to accompany the men without hesitation. The source describes his response to the summons; the earlier command also gives the Spirit's sending explanation, which is not a new speech quoted in his later question.

Cornelius recalls a ninth-hour prayer and a man in shining clothing, corresponding to the narrator's ninth-hour vision of an angel. Four-days-ago, prayer and clothing are specified in the report; no fasting clause or identical visitor-description wording is added to either unit.

Cornelius' reported prayer-heard/alms-remembered message corresponds to the angel's earlier prayers-and-alms memorial statement. The paired themes match while the reporting voice and heard/remembered versus ascended wording remain distinct.

The report combines the earlier command to summon Simon Peter from Joppa with the Simon-the-tanner seaside address. It keeps guest and host distinct and supplies no extra speech promise absent from these saved initial instructions.

Cornelius welcomes hearing all the Lord has commanded Peter; Peter later reports the angel's promise of words for Cornelius and his household's salvation. The latter promise is additional to Acts 10's quoted summons, and the audiences and statement forms are not made identical.

Peter declares God shows no partiality; Deuteronomy describes the Lord as showing no partiality and taking no bribe. The shared divine-character claim supplies scriptural background, while Peter's present recognition and Gentile encounter remain their own narrative context.

Peter says God accepts those fearing Him and practicing righteousness in every nation; Romans describes glory, honor and peace for good-doers, Jew and Greek, and no divine partiality. The contexts and precise criteria remain distinct, not a substituted complete formula.

Peter describes God sending Israel the peace message through Jesus Christ, Lord of all; Ephesians describes Christ proclaiming peace to far and near hearers. Sender, proclaimed message and the differing audience formulations are preserved rather than turned into one identical statement.

Both place Jesus' ministry in Galilee in relation to John's activity. Acts refers to the baptism John proclaimed and what took place throughout Judea, beginning from Galilee; Mark explicitly says after John was handed over and names Jesus' kingdom announcement. The distinct time markers are not equated.

Peter explicitly attributes Jesus' anointing with the Holy Spirit and power to God. Luke has Jesus read the Spirit-and-anointing passage with release and sight imagery and declare its present fulfillment. The reading and ministry summary have different forms and do not list identical beneficiaries.

Both speeches involving Peter name Jesus' killing by hanging on a tree and witness testimony. The council address uses you; the Caesarea speech uses they. The changed audiences and pronouns are kept, without assigning Cornelius or every Jewish person the same narrated action.

Peter proclaims God's raising Jesus on the third day and granting appearances; Luke's resurrection announcement recalls Jesus' third-day prediction. The target supports the resurrection/day correspondence without independently describing all the appearances mentioned by Peter.

Peter says selected witnesses ate and drank with the risen Jesus; Luke narrates disciples giving Jesus fish and Him eating before them. The shared meal setting does not make Luke explicitly narrate their eating, drinking or every appearance and participant in Peter's summary.

Peter says Jesus commanded proclamation and God appointed Him judge of living and dead. The letter's charge likewise names Christ Jesus judging living and dead and urges word proclamation. Commissioning voices, recipients and temporal expressions remain distinct.

Peter joins prophetic witness, believing and forgiveness through Jesus' name; Jesus' concluding instruction joins scriptural fulfillment with repentance and forgiveness proclaimed in His name to all nations. Believing and repentance, speakers and stated scriptural scope are retained without inventing a list of every prophecy.

Peter later recounts the Spirit falling on the hearers and compares the beginning. Acts 10 says while he was still speaking these words; Acts 11 says as I began to speak. Those distinct timing expressions remain rather than being converted into an identical transcript.

The circumcision believers accompanying Peter marvel at the Spirit's outpouring on Gentiles; his later report calls it the same gift, and Jerusalem hearers glorify God for Gentile repentance leading to life. The companion and Jerusalem audiences and their reactions are not collapsed.

Both narratives associate Spirit reception or filling with tongues speech. Pentecost specifies other tongues and Spirit-given utterance; Acts 10 says the listeners heard tongues and magnifying God. The target unit does not separately repeat that praise clause or identify the languages of this later scene.

Peter asks whether anyone can withhold water baptism from these Spirit recipients; the eunuch earlier asks what prevents his baptism when water appears. The shared obstacle-question form preserves different speakers, recipients and Spirit-sequence details, without supplying the absent Acts 8:37.

Both instructions link baptism with Jesus Christ's name. Acts 2 says upon the name, with repentance and a promised Spirit gift; Acts 10 says in the name after Spirit reception. The prepositions, hearers, sequence and additional request to stay are preserved rather than normalized.

deferred.reason: The named Freedmen's synagogue and regional membership are particular to this dispute notice. A generic dispute elsewhere does not identify this congregation or establish Saul's membership in it; no such association is inferred.

Simon's specific request that the others pray so the threatened things not happen is retained without forcing a different intercession request into his situation or deciding an unreported repentance, motive or outcome.

The Jerusalem disciples' initial fear and disbelief that Saul was a disciple are particular to this attempted joining. General apostolic contact or another person's objection does not closely reproduce this reaction; no extra encounter or emotional testimony is supplied.

The Cornelius and Samaria baptism/Spirit sequences, and in/upon/into name formulations, are not normalized.

Peter's selected witnesses eating and drinking with Jesus and Luke's Jesus eating before the disciples remain different reported statements. Belief, repentance, prophecy and forgiveness formulations are compared without supplying unquoted individual prophecies. Reported accusations, human-directed divine-status claims and audience reactions are not narrator endorsements or ethnic judgments.
